summary: Describes how to carry label mapping information for a route inside the same BGP Update message that announces the route. This lets routers distribute labels, such as those used in label-switched forwarding, together with routing information. It was replaced by RFC 8277.

eli5.summary: When you announce a street on a map, you also stick a small label on it in the same note, so nobody needs a second message.

questions: how to carry mpls labels in bgp
how does bgp carry mpls labels
subtitle: How BGP routers hand out MPLS labels in the same update message that announces the route.

tldr.problem: Routers that exchange routes with BGP also need to exchange the MPLS labels for those routes, and running a separate label distribution protocol for it is extra work.
tldr.mechanism: The label is piggybacked in the same BGP Update message as the route, inside the NLRI of the Multiprotocol Extensions attribute, with SAFI value 4 marking that a label is present.
tldr.outcome: Labels can ride along with routes, including through Route Reflectors. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 8277 and updated by RFC 6790.

today: RFC 3107 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8277 and updated by RFC 6790, so read those for the current rules.

sections.title: Labels Piggybacked on Routes
sections.content:
When BGP distributes a route, it can also distribute an MPLS label that is mapped to that route. RFC 3107 specifies how: the label mapping for a route is carried in the same BGP Update message that announces the route itself.

The RFC names situations where this helps. Two adjacent label switched routers that are also BGP peers can distribute labels without any other label distribution protocol. In a network with exterior and interior routers, the interior routers need not receive any BGP routes at all, as long as they support MPLS. And when speakers exchange routes through a Route Reflector, the Route Reflector can distribute the labels too, which the RFC says improves scalability quite significantly.

The mechanism uses the BGP-4 Multiprotocol Extensions attribute. A BGP speaker may not send labels to a peer unless that peer has said, through Capability Advertisement, that it can process Updates with the given SAFI.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending one letter about the road and another about its sign, you put both in the same envelope. Helpers in the middle can pass the envelope along without opening a second one.

sections.title: Encoding Labels in the NLRI
sections.content:
Label information travels as part of the NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) in the Multiprotocol Extensions attributes. The AFI gives the address family as usual, and SAFI value 4 indicates that the NLRI contains a label.

The NLRI is encoded as one or more triples of <length, label, prefix>:

  • Length is 1 octet and counts, in bits, the address prefix plus the label or labels.
  • Label carries one or more labels (a label stack). Each label takes 3 octets: the high-order 20 bits hold the label value and the low-order bit is Bottom of Stack.
  • Prefix holds the address prefix, followed by enough trailing bits to end on an octet boundary. The value of those trailing bits is irrelevant.

The labels for a route must be assigned by the LSR identified by the route's Next Hop attribute. A speaker that redistributes a route must not change its labels (except by omission) unless it changes the Next Hop.
sections.eli5: Each entry is a little package: how long it is, the sticker number, and the address. The sticker has to be handed out by the place the traffic is headed to.

sections.title: Withdrawals and Multiple Routes
sections.content:
A route and its label binding can be withdrawn in two ways: by advertising a new route and label with the same NLRI, or by listing the old NLRI in the Withdrawn Routes field of an Update. In the withdrawal, the label field should be set to 0x800000. Ending the BGP session also withdraws everything.

A speaker may keep and advertise more than one route to the same destination, as long as each route has its own label or labels. A single Update can carry several such routes. If a withdrawal names a label, only the route with that label is withdrawn. If it names no label, only the unlabeled route is withdrawn and the labeled routes stay.
sections.eli5: To take back a sign you either post a new one for the same spot or send a note that says cancel. If the note names a sign, only that sign goes away.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement and Adjacency
sections.content:
A speaker that carries labels in the Multiprotocol Extensions should use the Capabilities Optional Parameter to tell its peers. The MP_EXT capability code advertises the (AFI, SAFI) pairs available on a connection. A speaker should not advertise this capability to another speaker unless there is a Label Switched Path (LSP) between the two.

A speaker that can handle multiple routes to a destination should advertise that too, with a capability value of 4.

The RFC also explains why the LSP matters. In a chain A, B, C, D, if D gives A a label L, A cannot simply push L and send the packet to B. A must push another label distributed by B, and B and C swap labels in turn, so that D is the only router that sees L on top. The RFC does not specify any procedure to check this in real time. It treats this as an issue for network management and operation.
sections.eli5: Before you swap secret codes with a friend across town, you need a road that actually reaches them. This RFC leaves building and checking that road to the network operators.

sections.title: Label Spoofing Risks
sections.content:
On a point-to-point link, a router knows who sent each packet and can drop packets whose top label it never gave out. That prevents label spoofing, where a router imposes a label that was not properly distributed to it.

When peers are separated by an MPLS network, or Route Reflectors are in use, that check no longer works because the receiver cannot tell who pushed the top label. The RFC suggests other techniques. If labeled packets are never accepted from external interfaces and all BGP-distributed labels are advertised via IBGP, an untrusted router cannot inject labeled packets. A weaker condition is enough: any labeled packet received on an external interface must carry a top label that was actually distributed out that interface.
sections.eli5: If anyone can walk in wearing any badge, the guard cannot tell real from fake. So the network only lets in people who came through doors where the badges were really handed out.
